blocks.text: Every month, oil royalties, company tax and VAT flow into the Federation Account. Then the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) shares the pool among the Federal Government, the 36 states and the local governments. How that money is raised, how it is spent, and what happens when spending outruns revenue, is public finance — the government's own income-and-expenditure account.

blocks.markdown:
**Public finance** studies how government obtains, spends and manages money. Nigerian government revenue comes from **oil** (petroleum profit tax, royalties, gas, NNPC transfers), **non-oil taxes** (companies income tax, personal income tax at state level, VAT, customs and excise), **non-tax receipts** (fees, fines, rents, grants, profits of public enterprises) and **borrowing** when the rest is not enough.

Expenditure is split into **recurrent** spending — salaries, overheads, pensions and debt service that recur every year — and **capital** spending — roads, power plants, schools and other assets that add to the country's productive capacity. A budget that is almost all recurrent leaves little for growth.

blocks.title: The budget
blocks.text: A budget is a statement of planned government revenue and planned government expenditure for a given period, usually a year. It is **balanced** when the two sides are equal, a **surplus** when revenue exceeds expenditure, and a **deficit** when expenditure exceeds revenue. Nigeria has typically run deficits, covered by issuing domestic securities and by external borrowing.

blocks.caption: Name the budget by comparing the two totals — do not guess from the size of one figure alone

blocks.title: Identifying a deficit and the financing gap
blocks.prompt: A hypothetical federal budget estimates independent revenue and FAAC receipts of ₦4.50 trillion and total expenditure of ₦5.20 trillion, of which ₦3.80 trillion is recurrent and ₦1.40 trillion is capital. State the type of budget, the size of the gap, and the share of spending that is capital.

steps.text: Compare revenue with expenditure: ₦4.50 trillion against ₦5.20 trillion.
Expenditure exceeds revenue, so the budget is in deficit.
The deficit is ₦5.20 trillion − ₦4.50 trillion = ₦0.70 trillion (₦700 billion).
Capital spending is ₦1.40 trillion out of ₦5.20 trillion, which is 1.40/5.20 × 100 = 26.9 per cent, so most of the budget is still recurrent.
The ₦700 billion gap must be closed by internal debt (Treasury bills and bonds) or external debt, or by drawing down reserves — it does not disappear.

blocks.answer: Deficit budget of ₦700 billion; capital spending is about 27 per cent of the total

items: **Internal (domestic) debt** — naira securities held by the CBN, banks, pension funds and the public: Treasury bills (short-term) and FGN bonds (longer-term).
**External debt** — obligations in foreign currency to official creditors, multilateral bodies and holders of Eurobonds.
**Fiscal policy** — the deliberate use of tax and government spending to influence output, employment and prices.
**Expansionary fiscal policy** — tax cuts and/or higher spending, usually a larger deficit, to fight unemployment.
**Contractionary fiscal policy** — tax rises and/or spending cuts, moving towards surplus, to fight inflation.
**FAAC** — the monthly sharing of federally collected revenue; derivation payments extra-compensate oil-producing states, but the formula itself is not fiscal policy.

blocks.markdown: Public debt is not automatically a disaster: borrowing to build a refinery or a rail line can raise future income by more than the debt service. It becomes a burden when it finances consumption, when it is denominated in dollars while oil receipts falter, or when interest crowds out capital spending. Fiscal policy and monetary policy should point the same way — a CBN tightening is undermined if the budget is expanding demand at the same time.

blocks.title: Deficit is a flow; debt is a stock
blocks.text: This year's budget deficit is the extra borrowing needed now. Public debt is the pile of all past deficits not yet repaid. A country can run a deficit and still have a falling debt ratio if the economy (and tax base) grows faster than the new borrowing. Do not use the two words as synonyms.

points: Government revenue comes from oil, non-oil taxes, non-tax receipts and borrowing; FAAC shares federally collected funds.
Expenditure is recurrent (running costs and debt service) or capital (assets).
A budget is balanced, surplus or deficit according to whether revenue equals, exceeds or falls short of spending.
Public debt is internal or external; it finances deficits and is a stock built from past deficits.
Fiscal policy uses tax and spending: expansionary in a slump, contractionary against inflation.
